procedural_history.originating_court: First Court of Munsiff at Serampur
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated May 11, 1966 of the Calcutta High Court in Criminal Revision No. 188 of 1966.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Magistrate convicted the respondents under s. 441/447 I.P.C., and the conviction was affirmed by the Sessions Judge. But the High Court, on a revision, acquitted the respondents as it was of the view that the appellant was not in actual possession of the property and that the complainant must not only be in actual possession but also be present at the time of the trespass so as to bring the offence under s. 441/447 I.P.C.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed by special leave against the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court held that the High Court was in error and restored the judgment and order of the Magistrate.

directions: the judgment of the High Court set aside
the judgment and order of the Magistrate 1st Class Serampur, which was affirmed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Hoogly, restored

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant, who had obtained possession of a vacant piece of land through court proceedings, could be considered to be in 'actual possession' for the purposes of criminal trespass.

facts: The appellant filed a suit in 1951 and, after a lengthy legal process, obtained a decree of ejectment against the respondents.
In February 1963, a court official (Nazir), with police assistance, formally evicted the respondents and delivered 'actual physical possession' of the land to the appellant.
After the appellant took possession, the land was left vacant.
Two weeks later, the respondents trespassed onto this vacant land.
law: For a vacant piece of land, the person who has legally obtained possession is considered to be in 'actual possession'.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court was incorrect in its reasoning.

It reasoned that since the appellant had formally obtained possession of the land through a court-ordered eviction, and the land was subsequently lying vacant, the 'actual possession' must be considered to be with the appellant.
The fact that the land was vacant did not negate the appellant's possession which had been legally and physically established.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the appellant was in 'actual possession' of the vacant land because he had legally and physically obtained possession through court proceedings just two weeks prior to the trespass.

issue.issue_text: Whether the offence of criminal trespass under Section 441 IPC requires the person in possession to be physically present at the time of the trespass to establish an 'intent to annoy'.

facts: The appellant had obtained actual physical possession of a piece of land after a prolonged legal battle, evicting the respondents with police help.
Just two weeks after being evicted, the respondents trespassed back onto the land and began preparations to build structures.

The High Court had acquitted the respondents, reasoning that the appellant (the complainant) was not physically present at the time of the trespass, and therefore an 'intent to annoy' could not be established.
law: The Supreme Court explicitly stated that the law does not require the person in possession of the property to be physically present at the time of the trespass for the offence of criminal trespass to be made out.
To establish the offence, the court must be satisfied from the circumstances that the dominant intention or aim of the entry was to cause annoyance, intimidation, or insult.
application: The Court examined the circumstances of the case to determine the respondents' intention.
It noted that after a twelve-year legal battle and a recent forcible eviction, the respondents could have had no realistic hope of staying in possession of the land.
Given these facts, the Court concluded that there could be no other dominant intention for the trespass other than to annoy the appellant, who was the rightful possessor.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's reasoning, holding that the physical presence of the person in possession is not required to prove an 'intent to annoy' under Section 441 IPC. The Court found that the intent could be inferred from the circumstances and, in this case, the respondents' dominant aim was clearly to annoy the appellant. Consequently, it overturned the acquittal and restored the conviction.

issue.issue_text: Whether the respondents' entry onto the property was with the primary aim and intent to annoy the appellant, as required to constitute the offence of criminal trespass.

facts: After a 12-year legal battle that began in 1951, the appellant obtained a court order and, with police help, took actual physical possession of a piece of land from the respondents in February 1963.
Just two weeks after being evicted, the respondents trespassed back onto the same land.
The respondents were found on the land making preparations to build bamboo structures.
law: To establish the offence of criminal trespass, the court must be satisfied that the primary aim or "dominant intention" of the entry was to cause annoyance, intimidation, or insult.
It is not enough to simply show that annoyance was a likely consequence of the entry, even if the trespasser was aware of this likely consequence.
application: The Court examined the circumstances of the case to determine the respondents' primary aim.
It reasoned that after being evicted following a long and unsuccessful legal battle, the respondents could have had "no hope" of being able to successfully repossess and stay on the land.
Given the lack of any other plausible reason for the trespass, the Court inferred that the only "dominant intention" could have been to annoy the appellant, who had just legally won possession.

The Court also dismissed the High Court's reasoning, clarifying that the appellant was in actual possession of the vacant land and that the law does not require the person being annoyed to be physically present at the time of the trespass.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the respondents' entry onto the property was indeed with the primary aim and intent to annoy the appellant, thus satisfying the requirement for the offence of criminal trespass.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant, who had obtained possession of a vacant piece of land through court proceedings, could be considered to be in 'actual possession' for the purposes of criminal trespass.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that they were in 'actual possession' of the land, having obtained 'actual physical possession' through the execution of a court decree with the help of the Nazir and police on February 3, 1963. The fact that the land was vacant did not negate their possession.
respondent_arguments: The respondents' position, which was accepted by the High Court, was that the appellant was not in 'actual possession' of the property, likely because the land was vacant and the appellant was not physically occupying it at the moment of the trespass.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the offence of criminal trespass under Section 441 IPC requires the person in possession to be physically present at the time of the trespass to establish an 'intent to annoy'.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the law does not require the person in possession to be physically present at the time of the trespass for the offence to be constituted.
respondent_arguments: The respondents' argument, reflected in the High Court's judgment, was that the complainant must be present at the time of the trespass to establish the 'intent to annoy' required for an offence under s. 441/447 I.P.C.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the respondents' entry onto the property was with the primary aim and intent to annoy the appellant, as required to constitute the offence of criminal trespass.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the respondents' intention was clearly to annoy them. This was evidenced by the long history of litigation starting in 1951, the appellant obtaining possession only after a prolonged legal battle, and the respondents trespassing and starting construction just two weeks after being evicted, with no realistic hope of retaining possession.
respondent_arguments: The respondents' argument, inferred from their defense and the High Court's acquittal, would have been that their entry was not with the dominant intent to annoy the appellant, but for some other purpose (such as asserting a claim of right).

cases.case_name: Mathuri and Others v. State of Punjab
cases.principle: To establish that an entry on property was with the intent to annoy, intimidate, or insult, it is necessary for the Court to be satisfied that causing such annoyance, intimidation, or insult was the aim of the entry. It is not sufficient to merely show that annoyance was a likely consequence of the entry and that this was known to the person entering.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: To establish criminal trespass, the entry onto the property must be with the primary aim of causing annoyance, intimidation, or insult; it is insufficient that this is merely a known or likely consequence of the entry. Furthermore, the law does not require the person intended to be annoyed to be physically present at the time of the trespass, and a person who has legally obtained possession of vacant land is considered to be in actual possession.
obiter: The court's opinion that the Magistrate's sentence was too lenient and that a sentence of imprisonment should have been considered.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the respondents' entry onto the property constituted criminal trespass because their dominant intention was to annoy the appellant. This intention was inferred from the surrounding circumstances, specifically the long history of litigation, the appellant having just obtained possession through a court order after 12 years, and the respondents trespassing and starting construction only two weeks later with no realistic hope of retaining the land. The court held that under these facts, no other dominant intention for the trespass could be found.
legal_tests_applied: To establish that an entry on property was with the intent to annoy, intimidate, or insult, the court must be satisfied that causing such annoyance, intimidation, or insult was the 'aim of the entry'. In deciding this, the court must consider all relevant circumstances, including the probability of an alternative 'dominant intention' which prompted the entry. It is not sufficient to merely show that annoyance was a natural consequence of the entry.
policy_considerations: The court expressed a view that sentences should be sufficient to deter 'inveterate trespassers' who repeatedly and willfully defy court orders, noting that the Magistrate was 'rather lenient' for only imposing a fine and should have sentenced the main respondent to imprisonment, however short.
